Question: Describe the current responsibilities of all three teams, and explain the org changes that produced this structure, step by step.
response_text:
**Current Responsibilities of the Three Teams** | Team | Primary Scope | Typical Deliverables | Key Inter‑team Interactions | |------|----------------|----------------------|-----------------------------| | **Frontend Team** | All client‑facing UI/UX work. | • Web and mobile UI components
• Interaction design & accessibility
• UI‑state management (e.g., Redux, Vuex)
• Integration of UI with backend APIs (consumption only)
• Front‑end testing (unit, visual regression, e2e) | Works closely with the Backend team to consume APIs and with the Platform team when it needs environment provisioning (dev/staging URLs, feature‑flag services, CDN configuration). | | **Backend Team** | Business‑logic layer and public APIs. | • Design & implementation of domain services
• REST/GraphQL/gRPC API contracts
• Data‑validation, authorization, and business rules
• Persistence logic (ORM, data‑access layer)
• API versioning, documentation (OpenAPI/Swagger) | Relies on the Platform team for underlying infrastructure (databases, message brokers, CI/CD pipelines, observability). Provides contracts that the Frontend team consumes. | | **Platform Team** (carved out of Backend) | All infrastructure, tooling, and runtime concerns that support the product. | • Cloud‑resource provisioning (IaC – Terraform, CloudFormation)
• CI/CD pipelines, release automation
• Container orchestration / serverless runtimes
• Monitoring, logging, tracing, alerting
• Security hardening, secret management, networking, DNS, CDN, caching layers
• Service‑mesh / API‑gateway configuration | Supplies the Backend team with managed environments (dev, test, prod) and the runtime platform they run on. May also provide shared services (auth, feature‑flag, rate‑limiting) that both Frontend and Backend consume. | --- ### Step‑by‑Step Evolution of the Organization | Phase | Organizational Shape | Reason for Change | Resulting Team Focus | |-------|----------------------|-------------------|----------------------| | **1. Single “Full‑Stack” Team** (initial state) | One team owned **both** the UI layer and the server‑side logic. | Early stage – product was small, the codebase was manageable by a handful of engineers, and there was no need for deep specialization. | Everyone wrote UI, API endpoints, and handled the underlying servers. | | **2. Split into Frontend + Backend** (first re‑org) | Two dedicated squads:
• **Frontend** – UI/UX, client‑side code.
• **Backend** – server‑side services & APIs. | The product grew, the codebase became large enough that specialization improved velocity and quality. Separate skill sets (design/JS frameworks vs. Java/Node/Python, databases, etc.) could be recruited and nurtured. | Frontend focused on delivering a polished user experience; Backend focused on robust, scalable business‑logic services. Infrastructure (servers, CI/CD) was still owned by the Backend team. | | **3. Carve out a Platform Team from Backend** (second re‑org) | Three squads:
• **Frontend** (unchanged)
• **Backend** (now “Business Logic” only)
• **Platform** (infrastructure & dev‑ops) | As the organization scaled further, the operational load (cloud provisioning, CI/CD, monitoring, security, cost‑management) out‑grew what a pure development team could handle efficiently. A dedicated team could adopt best‑in‑class tooling, enforce standards, and provide self‑service capabilities. | Backend stopped managing servers, databases, or CI pipelines and concentrated on domain logic and API design. Platform took over all infra‑as‑code, runtime environments, observability, and reliability engineering. | | **4. Stabilized Structure** (current) | **Three clearly delineated responsibilities** (as described in the table above). | The separation aligns with the **“Three‑Tier”** architecture (Presentation → Application → Infrastructure) and supports independent scaling of each function:
• Frontend can hire UI/UX specialists without needing deep ops expertise.
• Backend can hire domain engineers focused on business value.
• Platform can hire SRE/DevOps engineers who own reliability and cost. | Each team now has a well‑defined charter, reduces overlap, and enables faster delivery cycles. | --- ### How the Changes Produced the Present Structure 1. **Growth → Need for Specialization** - The product’s user base and feature set expanded, making the “full‑stack” approach a bottleneck. - Splitting into Frontend and Backend allowed each group to deepen expertise and adopt tooling specific to their domain (e.g., React/Vue vs. Spring Boot/Express). 2. **Operational Complexity → Dedicated Platform** - With more services, databases, and environments, the Backend team’s operational duties (provisioning, CI/CD, monitoring) began to consume a large portion of their capacity. - By extracting those duties into a **Platform** team, the organization created a “service‑provider” layer that could standardize infrastructure across all product services. 3. **Resulting Clear‑Cut Ownership** - **Frontend**: owns the user‑facing experience; no responsibility for servers or deployment pipelines (except for front‑end build artefacts, which the Platform team hosts). - **Backend**: owns the *what* (business rules, data contracts) and the *how* (API implementation), but relies on Platform for the *where* (runtime environment). - **Platform**: owns the *where* (cloud resources, CI/CD, observability) and provides reusable platform services (auth, feature flags, logging) that both Frontend and Backend consume. This three‑team arrangement is now the operating model: each team can iterate independently, measure its own success metrics (e.g., UI performance, API latency, deployment frequency), and collaborate through well‑defined contracts (API specs, service‑level agreements, shared platform APIs).
